10 units, each with worked examples, a 10-mark practice set in CBSE question styles, common mistakes and quick recall

How this book matches your board exam. Research check: this book follows the CBSE Class 10 Mathematics syllabus for 2026–27 (Standard 041 and Basic 241).

  • Real Numbers: the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, and proofs of the irrationality of √2, √3, √5 and similar numbers. This is the Number Systems unit, worth 6 marks.
  • Polynomials: zeroes of a polynomial, and the relationship between the zeroes and coefficients of quadratic polynomials. This is part of the Algebra unit, worth 20 marks together with linear equations, quadratic equations and arithmetic progressions.

The theory paper is 80 marks in 3 hours: 38 questions in five sections (1-mark MCQs and assertion–reason, 2-, 3- and 5-mark answers, and case studies), with internal choice, plus 20 internal marks. The question paper design is unchanged from 2025–26.

Each unit ends with a 10-mark practice set in these question styles. Every number in this book has been checked by computer. The marking points are our own, not the official CBSE marking scheme. Check the latest sample paper on cbseacademic.nic.in.

Unit 1 of 10: Number System Review and Prime Factorisation

Key ideas

  • Natural numbers 1, 2, 3, …; whole numbers 0, 1, 2, …; integers …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
  • Rational numbers can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Irrational numbers cannot, for example √2, √3 and π. Rational and irrational numbers together make the real numbers.
  • A prime number has exactly two factors (1 and itself). A composite number has more than two. 1 is neither prime nor composite.
  • Prime factorisation: write a number as a product of primes using a factor tree or repeated division.

Worked examples

Example 1: 140 = 2 × 70 = 2 × 2 × 35 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 7, so 140 = 2² × 5 × 7.

Example 2: 3825 = 3 × 1275 = 3 × 3 × 425 = 3 × 3 × 5 × 85 = 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 × 17, so 3825 = 3² × 5² × 17.

Example 3: 7429 = 17 × 19 × 23. Test divisibility by primes in order; 7429 is not divisible by 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 or 13, but 7429 ÷ 17 = 437 = 19 × 23.

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark) Which is irrational? (a) 0.25 (b) 22/7 (c) √5 (d) −3. Answer: (c).
  2. (1 mark) Is 1 a prime number? Answer: no; it has only one factor.
  3. (2 marks) Express 156 as a product of its prime factors. Answer: 156 = 2 × 78 = 2 × 2 × 39 = 2² × 3 × 13 (method 1, answer 1).
  4. (3 marks) Express 5005 as a product of prime factors, showing your working. Answer: 5005 ÷ 5 = 1001; 1001 ÷ 7 = 143; 143 ÷ 11 = 13. So 5005 = 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 (working 2, answer 1).
  5. (3 marks) Classify 0, −7, 3/4, √3 and π as whole numbers, integers, rational or irrational (each can be in more than one group). Answer: 0: whole, integer, rational; −7: integer, rational; 3/4: rational; √3 and π: irrational (3 marks for all correct, deduct 1 per error).

Common mistakes

  1. Calling 1 a prime. 2. Stopping the factor tree at a composite number. 3. Writing 22/7 as irrational (it is rational; π is irrational). 4. Forgetting powers: writing 2 × 2 instead of 2². 5. Missing that 0 is a whole number.

Quick recall

  1. Define a rational number. 2. Smallest prime number? 3. Prime factorise 140. 4. Is π rational? 5. Is every integer rational?

Answers: 1) A number of the form p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0. 2) 2. 3) 2² × 5 × 7. 4) No. 5) Yes.
